extracted.intended_audience: students, playwrights, poets, and scholars of poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic and dramatic works (especially tragedy), explaining essential elements (plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, song), genre distinctions, and formal requirements such as unity of action and appropriate meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal differences of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The three differences which distinguish artistic imitation are the medium, the objects, and the manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medium = rhythm, tune, metre, language, etc.; Objects = kinds of men (better, worse, as they are); Manner = narration (speaker) or presentation (characters acting). These three axes determine genre distinctions (e.g., tragedy vs. comedy vs. epic). Examples: dancing imitates by rhythm alone; some arts employ all means (rhythm, tune, metre) such as dithyrambic poetry, tragedy and comedy at times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts differ with respect to the medium used—rhythm, tune, metre, language, movement, or combinations thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which media are employed (e.g., dance uses rhythm without harmony; tragedy often combines rhythm, tune and metre; some forms use language alone). The chosen medium shapes formal decisions like inclusion of song or reliance on diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (types of characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action, portrayed as better than, worse than, or as they are in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether characters are elevated, realistic, or degraded (Homer — men better; Cleophon — as they are; Hegemon/Nicochares — worse). The moral type portrayed is a key determinant of genre and tone (tragedy tends to portray better types; comedy worse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs. enactment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration (speaking in another persona or his own voice) or by presenting characters as living and acting before the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to tell events (epic/narrative) or to represent action directly (drama). This choice affects immediacy, dramatic effect, and classification as drama vs. epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy must present a whole, significant action enacted with appropriate poetic ornament (meter, melody), and aim at producing pity and fear so as to effect emotional purgation. Evaluate seriousness, completeness, magnitude, and the presence of rhythm/harmony/song in the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Diction (lexis), Thought (dianoia), Spectacle/Scenery (opsis), and Song/Melody (melopoiia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parts determine a tragedy's quality. Plot and Character constitute the objects of imitation; Diction, Song are media; Thought is the manner. Assess presence and quality of each part; note that some parts (song, diction) appear in particular segments (verse vs. sung sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (structure of incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot (arrangement of incidents) is the first principle of tragedy and the most important element determining its quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give priority to constructing a coherent, causally integrated plot with a clear beginning, middle, and end. Key devices—reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis)—are plot-based and central to emotional impact. A well-constructed plot often outweighs excellent diction or character portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot = imitation of action, not of men
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates actions (praxeis) and life (bios); action and its end (outcome) are paramount, while character is subsidiary to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes so actions drive the drama and reveal outcomes; character should serve the action rather than merely be depicted by speeches. Without action there is no tragedy, though tragedy could exist without richly drawn character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that by which we ascribe certain qualities to agents; it is the cause (with thought) from which actions spring and determines how agents will act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must have consistent qualities that explain their choices and deeds; however, characterization alone (well-crafted speeches) does not substitute for a strong plot. Evaluate ethical consistency and how character enables or constrains action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the capacity to say what is appropriate to the occasion—reasoning, argument, proof, or the expression of general truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought where characters prove points or express principles; evaluate the clarity and persuasive power of reasoning in speeches and how thought contributes to the development of the plot and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction means the metrical arrangement of words and the power of expression carried by named words; it includes the poetic shaping of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the aptness and metrical suitability of word choice, the effectiveness of phrasing, and the interplay of diction with meter and song. Diction should serve the action and the characters' nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song / Melopoeia
rubrics_metrics.description: Song (melody) is the musical element of the poem and is one of the chief pleasurable parts of tragedy, appearing in particular parts of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the quality, placement and effect of sung elements; melopoeia enhances emotional atmosphere and should harmonize with the diction and action. It is ranked among the major pleasing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle / Scenery (opsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle concerns the visual components (scenery, stagecraft) of a production; it is the least artistic part yet can be powerfully affecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize spectacle's emotional potency but treat it as a supplement to poetical and plot craftsmanship rather than the primary source of tragic effect. It should support the action rather than compensate for weak plot/character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and length of action (unity of time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy tends to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (unity of time) or only slightly exceed it; Epic action has no time-limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing tragedy, aim for temporal unity—keep the action compact and focused within a short span to increase intensity and unity; for epic/narrative poetry, time may be extended freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs. simple plots (reversal & recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most powerful emotional elements—reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis)—are parts of the plot and mark complex plots as superior in emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for complex plot structures that incorporate reversal and recognition when appropriate; these devices generate pity and fear and are central to cathartic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific meter and measure appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres and parts of a poem call for different metres and measures: epic uses hexameter, iambic is colloquial and suits dialogue, trochaic tetrameter belonged to an earlier satyric order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metre appropriate to the genre and the nature of the language (colloquial speech favors iambic). Meter influences tone and naturalness of speech—use it to match character and dramatic circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as imitation of the lower type (the ludicrous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates characters of a lower type; the ludicrous is a subdivision of the ugly, being a defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comic writing, portray defects that are harmlessly ridiculous rather than vicious or harmful; the comic element should produce laughter without invoking genuine pain. Comedy historically developed later and was treated less seriously at first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and natural causes of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from two natural instincts: the instinct of imitation (mimesis) and the instinct for harmony and rhythm; there is also universal pleasure in imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge imitation and rhythm as foundational impulses; use imitation and musical-rhythmic elements to engage audiences' pleasure in recognizing likenesses and patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared and distinct elements between Epic and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constituent parts are common to both epic and tragedy, but tragedy contains elements (and organizes them) in ways not all present in epic; epic is narrative in form and restricted to one metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing forms, ensure the presence of elements appropriate to the chosen mode: tragic enactment and musical/dictional ornament vs. epic narrative and a single metrical form. Knowing good tragedy informs epic composition and vice versa.
